missionPremise: The corpus carried one `max_height_ft` flag with three different meanings in the field and one placeholder number (999) that no city's code states, and `primary-source-verified` claimed atom-grade provenance for values that were read through a copy -- a mirror, a browser render, a transcription. Downstream, LDT's `derive.ts:221` passed `d.max_height_ft` through without reading the flag and its `/local-setbacks` route serialised the number raw, so Round Rock's stories-only districts reached a reader as 'max height 999 ft'. The dispatch exists because the LDT deploy of P-258's tables would have carried all of that to the live surface: the flag had to mean one thing, the copy channel had to have a state that does not overclaim, and no surface could print a placeholder as a limit.
completionPredicate: A stranger with a fresh clone and no credential can evaluate this: (1) corpus `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run` -> 9 files, 128 tests, 0 failures, including the new `p299-height-flag-and-state.test.ts` (14 tests) which runs the gate over EVERY shipped table, asserts the G7/G8 invariants on the shipped data, asserts the OT-2 population (170 rows) and re-derives each file's OT-1 note basis from its own quotes and values; (2) LDT `node <vitest> run lib/adapters` -> 43 files, 563 tests, 0 failures, including `p299HeightFlagAndState.test.ts`, whose first assertion is that LDT's constants, state list and rule outcomes EQUAL the corpus package's -- edit one repo alone and the other's suite fails; (3) the two falsifier scripts run the gate over all 43 tables in both repos and print 116 pre-change offenders (all G7) and 0 post-change; (4) `p299_f3_round_rock_envelope.mts` prints a pre-change `props.maxHeightFt = 999` with the literal string "999" in the envelope JSON and a post-change `null` with `not_specified.max_height = true` and no "999"; (5) the corpus PR's three CI checks and LDT's eleven are green at the heads named below. leave_behind.text: A housekeeping instruction in a dispatch's 'Where you work' block is as binding as the build items, and it is the one nobody re-reads at close. This lane registered neither clone as instructed, and its first close draft then asserted 'registered under the property seat' from memory -- a claim the register flatly contradicts (no p299 entry exists). Re-derive every housekeeping claim at close from the file the instruction names (`git grep -n '<lane>' -- _catalog/seat_register.json`) rather than restating the instruction as an outcome.

A red check that dies EARLY can hide a real failure in the packages it never reached. On this lane the Test job failed at 3m28s (against ~13m for a pass) on a flake in the first package alphabetically, so api-server never ran -- and the re-run, running the whole suite, surfaced this branch's real defect in api-server. Read the JOB DURATION against a passing run before concluding what a red check means; re-run rather than re-roll, and treat the second red as the one to diagnose.

Before pushing a change to an API response SHAPE, find the tests that assert the exact key set (`Object.keys(row).sort()` is the giveaway) and run them, even when they need a database. This lane's one unrunnable-locally api-server file was exactly that assertion, and it was the only thing CI caught. Standing up a throwaway pgvector+postgis container and `pnpm --filter @workspace/db run push` took ten minutes and converted a blind spot into a covered one.

lib/submission-classifier/src/__tests__/upsert.test.ts times out at the 10s default while doing schema setup plus two seeded inserts (it also times out against a local Postgres with the file byte-identical to the base commit). Do not try to A/B a test at an older commit by adding a git worktree and junctioning node_modules into it on Windows: pnpm's resolution depends on the real path, so vitest dies with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Use the base commit's file contents in a working tree that has real installed deps, or accept the weaker-but-decisive evidence (`git diff <base> -- <package>` empty plus a local reproduction).

The 40 clearings split 6 by the row's own quote and 34 by the P-146 REAL_VALUE_FLAGGED classification.

Measured 2026-09-17: the corpus gate ALREADY blocked all 116 pre-change rows on G7 (present since 2026-09-07) and the rows shipped anyway, because no test ran the gate over a shipped table. LDT's hand-vendored copy of the same gate had no G7 and blocked none of them. So the same defect can be caught-by-a-rule and still be live: a rule that nothing runs is not a gate. Both repos now run the gate over every shipped table in CI.

Two hand-vendored copies of one contract drift silently in the direction nobody tests. LDT's gate.ts was missing a rule the corpus gate had carried for ten days. Pin the shared identifiers, the state list and the rule OUTCOMES as assertions in the consuming repo (this lane's p299HeightFlagAndState.test.ts does), so that editing one repo alone fails the other's suite -- a shared module would be better, but a divergence test is what a lane can ship without a refactor.

A sentinel that means 'not stated' must not be a number the consumer can compare against. 999 is a legal value for a number-typed field and 999 ft is a legal height, so every reader that trusts the type (engine atom-chain-to-facets.ts:607 emits any positive number; LDT's derive.ts:221 passed it straight through) reads it as a limit. A boolean flag is enforceable in a schema; 999 is enforceable only in prose, and prose does not survive a serialisation boundary.

A claim a change makes ABOUT ITSELF drifts exactly like a value does, and nothing in the gate, the tests or CI can see it -- they read values and flags, never prose. The 40 row decisions here were right and were the ruling's own pre-registered answer; the sentence describing WHY was false for 34 of them. It was found only by pointing a second mechanism (a regex over the quotes) at a claim the first mechanism (the reconciler) had written, and both repos now carry a test that re-derives the claim from the shipped data. Budget for a prose-audit pass on any note block a script writes.

'Treat it as absent (no number, with the reason)' is two requirements, and the second is the one that gets dropped. A bare `null` on the wire cannot be told from a field that failed to load or a table that never carried a value -- the ambiguity the change existed to remove reappears one layer out. If a surface must report an absence, put the reason in a FIELD, not in a spec description that no caller sees at runtime.

Do not take 'the pre-change state' from HEAD~N in an evidence script. It is correct only until the lane's second commit, after which it silently compares the change against itself -- this lane's falsifier-3 script printed a vacuous 'FALSIFIED: NO' that way, and it is indistinguishable from a real answer unless you read the script. Take an explicit SHA (--before-rev), and re-run every artifact after any new commit.

Do not hand-edit orval-generated client files, even when the edit is trivially derivable from a spec change. Run the repo's own codegen (`pnpm --filter @workspace/api-spec codegen`): it took 26s and proved the earlier hand edit was byte-identical to the generated output, which is the only way to know that rather than believe it.
